title: How a $700 tool sold into hospitals that already owned a million-dollar competitor
summary: Jason tells how, while selling environmental-monitoring hardware at ITWatchDogs, he found a hospital using a tiny bootstrapped product alongside HP OpenView. The lessons: price so procurement is a non-event, define the market by an individual's need rather than company size, ask customers about adjacent products to learn their life and channels, and land small then expand.

principles.text: When selling to businesses, price for procurement pain, not buyer psychology; stay under the no-approval threshold.
principles.quote: when you're selling to businesses--especially mid-sized to large businesses--it's less about the psychology of the buyer but rather how much of a pain in the ass it is for the buyer.

principles.text: A price under the credit-card limit is effectively free, so customers buy even if you add only a little incremental value.
principles.quote: you understand that $500 is not the same as $499.99; it's the same as $0.

principles.text: Customers will buy a second product for a problem already "solved"; you needn't beat the incumbent head-on.
principles.quote: What's Up Gold would never win against that line-up. But it doesn't matter--they sold their product to the same customer anyway.

principles.text: Define your target market by an individual's need, not "SMB" versus "Enterprise."
principles.quote: A target market defined by the needs of an individual IT person, not "SMB" vs "Enterprise."

principles.text: Ask customers about adjacent products and their daily life; they are more honest and reveal distribution channels you'd never guess.
principles.quote: we learned a lot about the customer even though it wasn't questions about our product.

principles.text: Enterprise sales can start small and affordable, then expand once you're a proven quantity.
principles.quote: It's not always a large top-down deal; it can start small, start accessible, start simple, start affordable, and then expand outward once you're a proven quantity.
